sentences.quote: Expenses not directly related to any one member of a household, such as the cost of food for the household, must be divided among the members of the household.
If you live with a person rent free in that person’s home, you must reduce the amount you provide for support of that person by the fair rental value of lodging the person provides you.
The total fair rental value of a person’s home that the person owns is considered support contributed by that person.
If you don’t provide the total lodging, the total fair rental value must be divided depending on how much of the total lodging you provide.
Property provided as support is measured by its fair market value.
Medical insurance premiums you pay, including premiums for supplementary Medicare coverage, are included in the support you provide.
Medical insurance benefits, including basic and supplementary Medicare benefits, aren’t part of support.
Amounts veterans receive under the GI Bill for tuition payments and allowances while they attend school are included in total support.

If you pay someone to provide child or dependent care, you can include these payments in the amount you provided for the support of your child or disabled dependent, even if you claim a credit for the payments.
The following items aren’t included in total support.
In figuring a person’s total support, include tax-exempt income, savings, and borrowed amounts used to support that person.

If you make a lump-sum advance payment to a home for the aged to take care of your relative for life and the payment is based on that person’s life expectancy, the amount of support you provide each year is the lump-sum payment divided by the relative’s life expectancy.
If you are in the trade or business of providing foster care, your unreimbursed expenses aren’t considered support provided by you.

If you aren’t in the trade or business of providing foster care and your unreimbursed out-of-pocket expenses in caring for a foster child were mainly to benefit an organization qualified to receive deductible charitable contributions, the expenses are deductible as charitable contributions but aren’t considered support you provided.
The year you provide the support is the year you pay for it, even if you do so with borrowed money that you repay in a later year.

claims.why_uncovered: The support question lists several measurement rules (fair rental value of lodging, TANF, military allotments, foster care payments, state benefits, the child's wages, scholarships). It leaves out the rules on dividing household expenses, the rent-free offset, a person's own home, items excluded from total support (income and payroll taxes, life insurance, funeral expenses), insurance premiums and benefits, GI Bill amounts, tax-exempt income and borrowed amounts, home-for-the-aged lump sums, foster-care business or charitable expenses, and the year support is provided. No question or refusal addresses these rules.

sentences.quote: In figuring a person’s total support, include tax-exempt income, savings, and borrowed amounts used to support that person.
Amounts veterans receive under the GI Bill for tuition payments and allowances while they attend school are included in total support.
Because the car is bought and owned by your child, the car’s fair market value ($4,500) must be included in your child’s support.
The total fair rental value of a person’s home that the person owns is considered support contributed by that person.
Survivors’ and Dependents’ Educational Assistance payments used for the support of the child who receives them.
If spouses each receive benefits that are paid by one check made out to both of them, half of the total paid is considered to be for the support of each spouse, unless they can show otherwise.

claims.quote: In figuring a person’s total support, include tax-exempt income, savings, and borrowed amounts used to support that person. / Amounts veterans receive under the GI Bill for tuition payments and allowances while they attend school are included in total support. / Because the car is bought and owned by your child, the car’s fair market value ($4,500) must be included in your child’s support. / The total fair rental value of a person’s home that the person owns is considered support contributed by that person. / Survivors’ and Dependents’ Educational Assistance payments used for the support of the child who receives them. / If spouses each receive benefits that are paid by one check made out to both of them, half of the total paid is considered to be for the support of each spouse, unless they can show otherwise.
claims.why_uncovered: The own-support question covers own funds actually spent, wages, lodging at fair rental value, foster payments, scholarships and social security benefits. It does not say that borrowed amounts (such as student loans), GI Bill amounts and property bought with the child's own funds count as the child's support. It also omits that Survivors' and Dependents' Educational Assistance payments and the other listed items are excluded from total support.

sentences.quote: For this purpose, a person isn’t a taxpayer if the person isn’t required to file a U.S. income tax return and either doesn’t file such a return or files only to get a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid.

A child isn’t the qualifying child of any other taxpayer and so may qualify as your qualifying relative if the child’s parent (or other person for whom the child is defined as a qualifying child) isn’t required to file an income tax return and either: • Doesn’t file an income tax return, or • Files a return only to get a refund of in- come tax withheld or estimated tax paid.
If the persons the child does live with aren’t U.S. citizens and have no U.S. gross income, those persons aren’t “taxpayers,” so the child isn’t the qualifying child of any other taxpayer.

claims.quote: For this purpose, a person isn’t a taxpayer if the person isn’t required to file a U.S. income tax return and either doesn’t file such a return or files only to get a refund of withheld income tax or estimated tax paid. / A child isn’t the qualifying child of any other taxpayer and so may qualify as your qualifying relative if the child’s parent (or other person for whom the child is defined as a qualifying child) isn’t required to file an income tax return and either: • Doesn’t file an income tax return, or • Files a return only to get a refund of in- come tax withheld or estimated tax paid. / If the persons the child does live with aren’t U.S. citizens and have no U.S. gross income, those persons aren’t “taxpayers,” so the child isn’t the qualifying child of any other taxpayer.
claims.why_uncovered: The question asks whether the person meets the conditions to be the qualifying child of any other person. It never applies the rule that a person who isn't required to file, and doesn't file or files only for a refund, is not a 'taxpayer'. As a result, a qualifying relative whose only other claimant is such a non-filer, or a child in Canada or Mexico living with non-taxpayers, would be wrongly excluded.

sentences.quote: You may be eligible to file as head of household even if the child who is your qualifying person has been kidnapped.
You can claim head of household filing status if all the following statements are true.
The child is presumed by law enforcement authorities to have been kidnapped by someone who isn’t a member of your family or the child’s family.
In the year of the kidnapping, the child lived with you for more than half the part of the year before the kidnapping.
In the year of the child’s return, the child lived with you for more than half the part of the year following the date of the child’s return.
You would have qualified for head of household filing status if the child hadn’t been kidnapped.
A person can’t qualify more than one taxpayer to use the head of household filing status for the year.
If the child isn’t claimed as your dependent, enter the child’s name in the entry space below qualifying surviving spouse.

claims.why_uncovered: hoh_eligible is built from the unmarried and home-cost questions and the Test 1 and Test 2 person counts. It refuses only temporary absences that head of household does not count and community property. Nothing asks about the kidnapped-child rule, which makes a kidnapped child count as living with you, and nothing refuses it. Nothing checks that the qualifying person has not already qualified another taxpayer for head of household. Nothing provides for entering the name of a qualifying child who is not claimed as a dependent.
